name: r2-all-2
statement: The base's accuracy at a sampling setting is set by the per-token surprise of the text it generates relative to one optimum: below it, a restatement that holds its probability in one sequence beats a progress step whose mass is split over many paraphrases and then self-reinforces into a loop (boredom trap), above it the text drifts (confusion trap); the opening cue moves the base into a lower-entropy deliberative mode, which is why the cue loops more than the plain prompt at T 0.6, is worth far more at T 1.0, and why any mode-sharpening truncation (top-p < 1) costs the cued base but helps the plain base at T 1.0.
scope: Olmo-3-1025-7B base, plain and cued, on MATH-500 and the 328 at cap 16,384, sampling with temperature 0.6-1.2 and top-p or similar truncation, grader v3. Covers cap hits, loops and the cue-by-temperature interaction. It does not cover RL's own mechanism (RL is outside the law because it concentrated the progress mass at forks, so it is insensitive to temperature), the non-cap errors that remain at T 1.0, or weight edits.

explains.how: At T 0.6 with top-p 0.95 the cued base's text is far below the optimum surprise and most long answers fall into a repeated block.
Removing top-p restores the diffuse tail where the progress steps live, raising surprise and cutting cap hits by 21.
At T 1.0 the cued mode's surprise sits near the optimum: no loops and little drift.
The plain base at T 0.6 has half the cued base's cap hits: its higher-entropy mode is nearer the optimum at T 0.6.
At T 1.0 the plain base is in the confusion trap and the cue pulls it back to the optimum, while at T 0.6 the cue gains only 3-10 points because it pushes the base into the boredom trap.

explains.quote: Plain base: T 1.0 - T 0.6 = -28.0, -29.6, -27.2, 0.0 by quartile
explains.how: Raising T moves the plain base into drift on every problem, a loss offset only on the longest problems, where it escapes loops.
On the 328 the same crossover holds: plain falls from 107 to 76 when T rises, cued rises from 119 to 164.
Harder problems produce more impasses, so the boredom trap at T 0.6 costs more cap hits on the 328 than on MATH-500.

explains.quote: the base's loops have periods of hundreds of characters
explains.how: The loops are repeated whole reasoning blocks (restatements), the sentence-level self-reinforcement the theory names, not token stutter.
Repetition self-reinforces with the number of copies already in context, so the base's own prefix, which already holds restatements, loops almost twice as often.

explains.quote: cuts limit loops 59 -> 53, T 1 cuts to 24
explains.how: The same ordering of truncation and temperature effects on loops holds in an unrelated model, as a sampler-independent surprise law predicts.

conflicts.how: At T 1.0 the cued base still has non-loop cap hits on RL-only problems; the theory calls these drift (confusion side) without independent evidence.
RL generates low-surprise text yet does not loop at T 0.6, so the surprise-to-repetition law is not shared across models; the theory has to exclude RL by assumption.

conflicts.quote: Rule-A loops: 0 of 500 in either cell
conflicts.how: With zero loops at T 1.0 the theory says nothing about the remaining 10.6-point gap there.

rival: Temperature is a plain noise-versus-sharpness trade-off with a monotone effect per model, and the cue simply adds a fixed amount of accuracy (no interaction with the sampler); top-p 0.95 at T 1.0 then removes junk tail tokens and helps both prompts slightly. Separation: under the rival, top-p 0.95 at T 1.0 raises or holds the cued base's score and does not add cap hits; under this theory it adds about 18 cap hits to the cued base and costs about 12 points, while it raises the plain base by about 38. The sign of the top-p effect flipping between prompts separates the two.

predictions.experiment: Base + opening cue, MATH-500 n=500, T 1.0 / top-p 0.95, cap 16,384, one sample, grader v3: cap hits
predictions.refuted_by: 30 or fewer cap hits (truncating the tail at T 1.0 does not bring loops back)

predictions.experiment: Same run (base + cue, MATH-500, T 1.0 / top-p 0.95): right
Plain base (no cue), MATH-500 n=500, T 1.0 / top-p 0.95, cap 16,384, one sample, grader v3: right (plain T 1.0 / top-p 1.0 is 224)
predictions.refuted_by: 232 or fewer right (truncation does not rescue the plain base from drift)

predictions.experiment: Base + opening cue, the 328 harder problems, T 1.0 / top-p 0.95, cap 16,384, one sample, grader v3: cap hits (top-p 1.0 gives 77)
Plain base (no cue), MATH-500 n=500, T 0.8 / top-p 1.0, cap 16,384, one sample, grader v3: right (T 0.6 gives 305-319, T 1.0 gives 224)
predictions.refuted_by: 268 or fewer right (no peak between T 0.6 and T 1.0; the plain base's accuracy falls linearly with T)

predictions.experiment: Teacher-forced under the base: mean per-token surprise (negative log-probability at T 1) of the cued base's 500 MATH-500 answers at T 1.0, after the cue, divided by that of the plain base's 500 answers at T 1.0 (existing answers)
predictions.refuted_by: ratio 1.0 or more (the cue does not move the base to a lower-entropy mode)

imports.finding: Repetition rate is a near-linear function of the observed cross-entropy of generated text, largely independent of the sampling method; too little surprise gives the boredom trap (repetition), too much the confusion trap (incoherence).
imports.how: Explains the cue-by-temperature interaction the team never explained (cue +38.6 at T 1.0 but small at T 0.6, cued base loops more than plain at T 0.6) and predicts that top-p 0.95 at T 1.0 has opposite signs for the cued and plain base.

imports.finding: Loops arise from risk aversion: when the progress action's mass is spread over alternatives and a cyclic action keeps its mass, sharpening (low T) picks the cyclic action; harder problems loop more; temperature removes loops but not errors.
imports.how: Explains why tail truncation (top-p 0.95), not only low temperature, adds loops (354 vs 378 at T 0.6), why the 328 shows more cap hits than MATH-500, and predicts loops return at T 1.0 under top-p 0.95.

imports.finding: The probability of repeating a sentence rises with the number of copies already in context and saturates; high-probability sentences reinforce faster.
imports.how: Explains why a started loop runs to the 16,384 cap and why the base loops more from its own prefix (38) than from RL's (21).
